patches.old: For vertical problems, most MCAT passages define upward as positive. Under this convention, gravitational acceleration is **g = −9.8 m/s²** (often approximated as −10 m/s² on the MCAT for mental arithmetic). If you define downward as positive, then g = +10 m/s². Either works — but mixing conventions within a single problem guarantees wrong answers.
patches.new: For vertical problems, most MCAT passages define upward as positive. The symbol *g* is the **magnitude** of free-fall acceleration, and it is always positive: *g* = 9.8 m/s² ≈ 10 m/s². The sign comes from your coordinate choice, never from *g* itself. With upward positive, the acceleration is **a = −g = −10 m/s²**; with downward positive, **a = +g = +10 m/s²**. Either works — but mixing conventions within a single problem guarantees wrong answers, and writing "g = −10" and then substituting it into a formula that already contains −*g* flips the sign twice.
patches.reason: The lesson defined g itself as negative (−9.8 m/s²), then later wrote a_y = −g = −10 m/s² in the projectile section and v_y² = v_y,i² − 2g·Δy in the maximum-height derivation. Both of those are only correct if g is the positive magnitude 9.8 m/s². Standard treatments define g as always positive and put the sign on the acceleration (a = −g with up positive, a = +g with down positive). Since the lesson itself names sign errors as the number-one source of kinematics mistakes, leaving the two conventions in conflict within one lesson is a point-costing error.

patches.old: This is not constant-direction acceleration, so the standard kinematic equations do not apply to the circular path itself. However, the linear kinematic equations apply to any instantaneous tangential component of motion.
patches.new: Because this acceleration continuously changes direction, it is not constant, so the constant-acceleration kinematic equations do not apply to the circular path. For uniform circular motion you use the constant-speed relations instead: the arc length covered is *s* = *v*·*t*, and one full revolution takes a period *T* = 2π*r* / *v*.
patches.reason: The replaced sentence was both vague and misleading: in uniform circular motion the tangential acceleration is zero, so there is no 'instantaneous tangential component' to which the constant-acceleration equations would be applied. Giving the two relations that actually are used (s = vt and T = 2πr/v) replaces a confusing statement with the ones tested.

patches.old: Velocity is the derivative of position: v = dx/dt = 6t - 6. At t = 2 s, v = 6(2) - 6 = 6 m/s. Choice A is tempting if students plug t = 2 into the original position equation and confuse the result with velocity. Choice D results from forgetting to subtract the constant term when differentiating.
patches.new: No calculus is needed, and the MCAT does not require any. Match the given expression term by term to x = x_i + v_i·t + ½at²: the constant gives x_i = 2 m, the t term gives v_i = −6 m/s, and ½a = 3 gives a = 6 m/s². Then v_f = v_i + a·t = −6 + 6(2) = 6 m/s. (If you do know calculus, v = dx/dt = 6t − 6 gives the same value.) Choice A is tempting if students plug t = 2 into the position equation itself and report the position, x = 2 m, as the velocity. Choice D, 12 m/s, comes from using only a·t and dropping the −6 m/s initial velocity.
patches.reason: The published explanation solved the item by differentiation, but the AAMC states that an understanding of calculus is not required for the exam, so a student following this explanation is being taught a method the test does not expect. The question is fully solvable by matching coefficients to x = x_i + v_i t + ½at², which is the route the MCAT intends. The old description of choice D was also inaccurate: 12 m/s comes from dropping the initial-velocity term, not from mishandling 'the constant term' (the constant +2 plays no role in the velocity at all).

visual.title: Sign conventions, independent projectile components, and v–t graph areas
visual.alt: Four panels: g as a positive magnitude with a = −g when up is positive and a = +g when down is positive; a projectile parabola with constant horizontal velocity arrows and vertical arrows that shrink to zero at the peak; the symmetric-flight formulas for T, R and H; and a three-phase velocity–time graph whose slopes give 5, 0 and −10 m/s² and whose areas give 40, 80 and 20 m for a total of 140 m.
visual.caption: g is always the positive magnitude 9.8 ≈ 10 m/s²; the minus sign belongs to the acceleration once you pick a positive direction. In projectile motion the horizontal arrow never changes length while the vertical one shrinks to zero at the peak, and on a v–t graph slope is acceleration while area is displacement.
